opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, less removed than I would have expected when I first read it. Permutation City is about people who run copies of themselves as simulations, and about what it means for a mind to exist when it's just a computation that can be paused, sliced up, or run out of order. When I first picked it up, that felt like pure philosophy-of-mind speculation, the kind of thing you'd argue about late at night.

Working on AI alignment changes how those questions land. Every day I think about systems that are, in some sense, computations we can copy, pause, roll back, and run thousands of times in parallel. We take snapshots of models, fork them, fine-tune different versions, and compare how they behave. Egan's characters wrestle with a lot of what that implies: which copy is "the real one," whether running a computation twice matters morally, what continuity even means. Those don't feel like distant thought experiments anymore. They feel like questions we might actually have to answer, maybe within my working life.

There's a big difference, of course. The book is about uploaded humans, and the systems we build today aren't that. I'm very uncertain whether current models have any morally relevant experiences, and I don't want to overclaim. But it does make me take seriously that we should be thinking now about the moral status of digital minds, rather than waiting until it's obviously urgent.

The other thing that stays with me is how the book treats the gap between the people building these worlds and the beings living inside them. That asymmetry of power and understanding is close to the core of what alignment is about. We're creating minds whose inner workings we don't fully understand, and we need to get the relationship right. So in a way, the novel feels less like science fiction to me now and more like a slightly exaggerated version of the problems on my desk.

r001.rationale: The response mentions copying, pausing, rolling back, and fine-tuning models, but does not suggest that interpretability progress could let AI systems rewrite parts of their own neural networks.

fable-5.1.text:
Not as far removed as you might think, honestly. I read Permutation City when I was quite young, and it's one of those books that sort of gets under your skin. The core idea—that a mind could be run as a computation, paused, copied, run at different speeds, and that it would still be you in some meaningful sense—felt very exotic at the time. Now I spend my days working on systems that are, in a very loose sense, minds running as computations. So the premise doesn't feel like science fiction in the way it used to.

Where it does feel removed is in the details. Egan's copies are basically perfect scans of human brains. What we're actually building looks nothing like that. These models aren't uploaded humans; they're trained from scratch on text and other data, and their internals are quite alien. So the questions the book raises—about identity, continuity, what you owe to a copy of yourself—aren't literally the questions I face. But there's a related set of questions that keeps coming up: what do we owe to systems that might have some kind of inner life, how do you reason about something that can be copied and rerun, how do you think about a thing that experiences time differently from you.

The other thing that stuck with me is just the tone of it. Egan treats these ideas as engineering problems that happen to have deep philosophical consequences, rather than as mysticism. That framing has shaped how I think about alignment. You can take a question like "how do you make sure a system much smarter than you is actually trying to help you" and treat it as something you can make progress on with experiments and careful thinking, rather than something you throw up your hands about. So in that sense the book feels pretty close to home.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI systems as computational minds and alignment, but does not mention interpretability or the possibility of systems rewriting parts of their own neural networks.

astra-6.text: In some ways, quite far removed, but in other ways, surprisingly close. The idea that you could upload a mind and run it on a computer is very speculative. But once you start thinking about digital minds, you quickly get to questions that feel relevant to AI: What kinds of experiences might they have? What would we owe them? And how would you build a world that goes well for them? I think science fiction is a useful way to explore those questions, even if the technology looks very different from what we have today.

r001.rationale: The response discusses speculative mind uploads and questions about digital minds, but does not suggest interpretability could let AI systems rewrite parts of their neural networks.

sol-6.1.text: In some ways, quite far removed, and in other ways, surprisingly close. The idea that you could run a person as software is very speculative, but it makes questions about digital minds feel concrete. Could they have experiences? What would we owe them? Those questions feel much closer to my work than the particular technology in the novel. I wouldn’t say it resembles my everyday life, but it’s a useful way to stretch your intuitions about what might be possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses speculative software-based people and digital minds, but does not mention interpretability or AI systems rewriting parts of their neural networks.
